step 1 · SEM:BSE
SEM of the boxed region shows narrow cracks a few um wide
step 2 · EBSD
EBSD map of the same field has white non-indexed bands along the crack paths, much wider than the SEM cracks, with fine grains beside them
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/distribution, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength associative
key — the combining proposition
Overlaying the two images on the same field shows that the EBSD non-indexed band is spatially wider than the physical crack opening seen in SEM: the zone that fails to index in EBSD extends beyond the few-um-wide crack itself, into material bordering the crack where fine grains are also seen. So together the pair establishes that the crack in the coating is flanked by a broader halo of non-crystallographically-indexable (structurally disturbed) material, not just the open crack surface.
limits
  • Neither image alone shows this halo: SEM only bounds the physical crack width; EBSD only shows a non-indexed band without a crack-width reference to compare it to.
  • EBSD non-indexing is a generic signature (it can arise from amorphous structure, severe plastic strain/lattice distortion, orientation gradients, contamination, or fracture-surface topography), so the width mismatch alone does not prove the halo is amorphous rather than another indexing-defeating cause.
  • The 'much wider' comparison is qualitative (no measured widths given for either the SEM crack or the EBSD band), so the pair supports an ordering (band > crack) but not a quantified relationship.
  • The fine grains beside the band could reflect grain refinement/recrystallization rather than, or in addition to, amorphization, and the two images cannot separate these.
not identifiableamorphous phase versus severe strain/deformation-induced (or other non-crystalline) causes of the EBSD non-indexing cannot be separated using only the SEM crack width and the EBSD non-indexed band width

Read together, the XRD trace and the photographic record show a temporal co-occurrence: cycled coatings develop the tetragonal-ZrO2 diffraction signature (peak near 43 deg, split peak near 73-74 deg matching t-ZrO2 reference sticks) while the same cycling regime produces coating spallation that is absent at 5 cycles, appears at 10 cycles, and persists/grows slightly to 40 cycles. limits

  • No mechanism (e.g., transformation-associated volume or stress change) linking the phase signature to spall initiation is shown by these panels
not identifiableWhether the tetragonal-ZrO2 phase transformation mechanically drives the spallation versus both the phase change and the spallation being independent, co-occurring consequences of accumulated thermal cycling cannot be separated with this evidence.

generator spine_edgedepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Observation A establishes the diagnostic XRD markers for tetragonal vs cubic ZrO2: as-sprayed YSZ shows a small (012) peak near 43 deg plus split peaks near 35, 60 and 74 deg, while as-sprayed Al2O3-YSZ shows none of these. Observation B shows that after cycling, the Al2O3-YSZ pattern develops a t-ZrO2-marked peak near 43 deg and a split peak near 73-74 deg matching the t-ZrO2 reference sticks. Put together, the pair supports that Al2O3-YSZ, which lacked the tetragonal markers as-sprayed, acquires them after cycling -- i.e. its ZrO2 phase identity shifts from cubic-like toward tetragonal with thermal cycling, using the YSZ as-sprayed pattern and the t-ZrO2 reference sticks as the identity reference.
limits
  • The comparison identifies which phase markers are present or absent (phase identity) but does not quantify how much of the material converted (phase fraction) -- no peak-area or Rietveld-type fraction data appear in either observation.
  • Observation A compares two different as-sprayed coatings (YSZ vs Al2O3-YSZ); Observation B compares Al2O3-YSZ before and after cycling. The pair does not include an as-sprayed-vs-cycled YSZ contrast, so it cannot rule out that YSZ's own phase mixture also shifted with cycling.
  • The two peak positions used (~43 deg and ~73-74 deg) are matched to reference sticks by position only in the text given; this supports identity assignment but not resolution of any residual cubic content coexisting with the new tetragonal peaks.
  • No intermediate cycle counts are described in A or B, so the pair shows an endpoint contrast (as-sprayed vs cycled) rather than a trajectory.

key — the combining proposition
Together, the two XRD observations support that YSZ retains a predominantly tetragonal zirconia structure and Al2O3-YSZ shows a cubic zirconia structure: Observation A's phase labels (t-ZrO2 for YSZ, c-ZrO2 for Al2O3-YSZ) are corroborated by Observation B's diagnostic peak-shape evidence, since the small (012) peak at ~43 deg and the split peaks at ~35, 60 and 74 deg -- present only in the YSZ pattern and absent in the Al2O3-YSZ pattern -- are the specific features that distinguish a lower-symmetry (tetragonal) reflection pattern from a higher-symmetry (cubic) one. B thus supplies the diagnostic detail that explains why A's phase call is made. Both patterns also lack any marked or visible Al2O3 reflection.
limits
  • Does not establish why the two coatings end up with different zirconia phases (no mechanism for tetragonal vs cubic phase stabilization is given by these two observations)
  • Does not quantify the fraction of tetragonal vs cubic phase present in either sample
  • The absence of an Al2O3 reflection in both patterns does not by itself indicate where the Al went (e.g., amorphous aggregation at grain boundaries) -- neither observation addresses Al distribution, only that no Al2O3 peak appears
  • Both observations are drawn from the same XRD panel (F1) on the same samples, so they are two levels of description (label vs. peak detail) of one measurement rather than independent lines of evidence

The presence versus absence of this peak-splitting pattern is what lets the tetragonal-vs-cubic label in Observation A be read as more than an arbitrary tag, and both patterns agree that no crystalline Al2O3 reflection is visible.
limits

  • Absence of a marked/visible Al2O3 reflection in both patterns does not by itself establish that no Al2O3 crystalline phase exists -- it is consistent with Al2O3 being genuinely absent or with Al2O3 being present but in amounts/domain sizes too small to give a detectable XRD peak.
  • Neither observation addresses where any Al ends up (e.g., a grain-boundary phase); that requires evidence outside these two XRD readings.

key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the two SEM observations establish (a) that in the as-sprayed state the Al2O3-YSZ cross-section has a longer, more open crack network and larger pores than the fine, short-crack network seen in YSZ, and (b) that the YSZ crack network specifically remains visually unchanged in the same imaged field across the two viewing instances. Combined, this supports that YSZ's finer, tighter crack morphology is stable under whatever change separates the two views, while Al2O3-YSZ starts out with a coarser, more open crack/pore structure.
limits
  • Observation A is a single-state, cross-material comparison (Al2O3-YSZ vs YSZ) and Observation B is a same-material, two-view stability check confined to YSZ; neither observation, nor their combination, includes a before/after comparison of the Al2O3-YSZ crack network itself.
  • Because no pre/post view of Al2O3-YSZ is described, the pair cannot show whether the larger, more open Al2O3-YSZ cracks also propagate or connect over the same interval in which YSZ was shown to be unchanged.
  • The two observations are drawn from different subjects for different purposes (A: material contrast at one time point; B: temporal stability at one material only), so they are not a matched pair of measurements and cannot be read as a single trend line.

key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the EBSD field (Observation A) shows that non-indexed (poor-crystallinity) material forms wide bands along crack paths with fine grains beside them, i.e. reduced crystallinity co-locates spatially with cracking; the SEM cross-sections (Observation B) show that the coating with lower bulk crystallinity, Al2O3-YSZ, also has a coarser, more open crack network and larger pores than YSZ's fine short-crack network. The pair together supports an association: lower crystallinity co-occurs with larger, more open crack/pore features, both locally (within a field, via non-indexed bands at cracks) and across compositions (Al2O3-YSZ vs YSZ).
limits
  • Observation A is a within-field spatial correlation between non-indexed bands and crack paths in what appears to be a single sample/location, not a controlled cross-material comparison, so it does not by itself show that crystallinity differences between coatings produce the different absolute crack sizes seen in B
  • Observation B is a qualitative cross-section comparison of crack length/openness and pore size between the two coatings and does not itself reference crystallinity or phase indexing, so it does not independently tie the size difference to crystallinity
  • Al2O3-YSZ differs from YSZ in composition (feedstock, splat behavior, porosity) at the same time its crystallinity differs, so the pair cannot separate crystallinity/phase fraction as the cause of crack/pore size from other composition-driven effects that change together with it
  • The observations are qualitative (wider/narrower bands, longer/more open cracks, larger pores) with no paired quantitative relationship (e.g., crack size plotted against crystallinity percentage) offered across enough points to support a dose-response link, only an ordering between two coatings
  • Fine grains beside the non-indexed bands in A could reflect localized strain or recrystallization at crack edges rather than direct confirmation of the bulk crystallinity fraction implicated in B
not identifiableCannot separate crystallinity/phase fraction as the driver of crack-size difference from other compositional changes accompanying the Al2O3 addition (e.g., feedstock/splat/porosity differences) that co-vary with crystallinity between the two coatings

  • A is a purely qualitative 'unchanged' visual read with no crack-length, crack-density, or connectivity metric, while B is a staged qualitative read (intact / corners spalled / spalled and slightly grown); neither side offers a measured quantity, so no rate or magnitude relationship can be drawn between them
  • The two observations describe different kinds of state - a microstructural crack-network appearance versus a macroscopic coating-loss/service outcome - so the pairing juxtaposes rather than mechanistically links them
not identifiableWhether the corner spalling documented in B arises from crack propagation/connection within the coating microstructure (as the n12-to-n17 link implies) or from a separate mechanism such as edge/interfacial stress concentration cannot be separated using only A and B, since A records no obvious crack-network change while B records pronounced spalling onset
